meta.imageAlt: Zetta: ask for the result and a team of bots does the rest. The Zetta robot sits at the center of four bots, and one of them needs you.
meta.title: Zetta: bots that work on your server while you do something else
meta.description: Zetta is a free, open source app that runs a team of bots on your own server. Tell Zetta what you need and come back to the result.

hero.lead: Zetta is a free, open source app that runs on your own server. Tell Zetta what you need, like a weekly summary or a code review. A team of bots does the work, and asks you only when it needs a decision.
hero.installLabel: One line on macOS, Linux or WSL
hero.note: A bot is a worker you set up, like Writer or Reviewer. It runs on an agent you already use: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more.
hero.robotAlt: The Zetta robot at the center of a graph. Four bots are connected to it and to each other, and a line runs from the robot to a cloud connected to GitHub, Notion, Cloudflare, Sentry and Linear. One bot waits for you. Illustration.
proof: Your data stays on your server

pain.before: Every agent you run is one more terminal to watch. Zetta puts them in one team on your server and
pain.mark: calls you only when one is stuck.

live.lead: A real recording of the app, with demo data. You describe a project. Zetta designs a small team of bots and asks you to approve each step.
live.note: Zetta in light mode, with demo data. Waiting time is sped up.
live.videoLabel: A recording of the Zetta app in light mode: Zetta designs a team of bots from a brief, and each step waits for approval. Demo data.

features.lead: Routines, memory, tasks and a desktop. Every clip below is the real app, with demo data.

tiles.title: Work that starts without you
tiles.body: Schedule a daily briefing, a weekly newsletter or a pull request review. The agenda syncs both ways with the main calendar of each Google account you connect.
tiles.alt: The routines page: a morning briefing, a Friday newsletter and a pull request queue, each with its next run. Demo data.

tiles.title: Nothing to explain twice
tiles.body: Bots keep notes from one chat to the next. Company knowledge is searchable, and the search can run on a model on your own server.
tiles.alt: Three notes a bot keeps in memory. Illustration.

tiles.title: A desktop on your server
tiles.body: Each bot can work on a Linux desktop that runs on your server. You set limits for memory, CPU and how many run at once.
tiles.alt: A recording of a bot using a computer and a terminal in the Zetta dashboard. Demo data.

tiles.title: Who has what, and what is stuck
tiles.body: Tasks move from backlog to in progress, blocked, review and done. Each card shows the bot that owns it.
tiles.alt: The task board with columns backlog, in progress, blocked and review, each card showing its bot. Demo data.

engines.lead: Each bot runs one of these agents, and each bot can use a different one.

groups.title: Connected apps
groups.body: Connect the accounts your bots need from Studio. Sharing a bot never shares your credentials.

groups.title: Your coding tools
groups.body: Claude Code or Cursor can work as a member of your team, through a built-in connection. They follow the same permission checks as the web app.

groups.title: Messaging
groups.body: Message your bots on Telegram, with your own bot token, or on WhatsApp, through your own WAHA server.

chief.lead: Zetta is your main bot, the chief of all the others. You talk to Zetta first. It sets up the other bots, hands out the work and keeps your routines running. It proposes, and you decide.

points.title: Ask for a result
points.body: No configuration screens to learn first. Say what you want done.

points.title: Every change is an Approve card
points.body: Zetta proposes a bot, a routine or a task. Nothing is created until you approve it.

points.title: Secrets stay out of the chat
points.body: When a bot needs a password or a key, Zetta opens a private form. The secret never goes through the conversation.

chief.alt: A chat with Zetta. The person asks for a weekly summary of their repositories, and Zetta proposes a Researcher bot with an Approve button. Illustration.
chief.ask: Every Monday, summarize what changed in our repositories and send me a brief.
chief.reply: I can set that up. I would add one bot for it:

fields.label: First task
fields.value: Summarize last week's merged pull requests

chief.orgAlt: The Zetta robot at the top as the chief, with four bots below it: Writer and Researcher are working, Reviewer is done, and Editor needs you. Illustration.

caps.title: Hire a bot
caps.body: Describe the role. Zetta proposes the agent, the access and the first task.

caps.title: Build a team from one brief
caps.body: A brief becomes several bots, each with its own job.

caps.title: Schedule routines
caps.body: Briefings and reviews that run on their own, when you say.

caps.title: Add skills and tools
caps.body: Give a bot what it needs: skills from the library, plugins, MCP servers and your connected apps.

caps.title: Open a room
caps.body: Put several bots and people in one conversation.

caps.title: Take secrets through a form
caps.body: Passwords and keys go into a private form, never into the chat.

install.lead: You need Git, OpenSSL and a running Docker or Podman. Zetta starts a web app, an API and a Postgres database.
install.note: Free under the MIT license. It is early: read the repository and its issues before you depend on it.

steps.title: Run the installer
steps.body: Works on macOS, Linux and WSL. It downloads Zetta, creates the two .env files with new secrets and starts the containers. Run it again to update.

steps.title: Finish setup in the browser
steps.body: Open http://localhost:3001 and paste the setup key from apps/server/.env. You become the admin of this install.

steps.title: Ask Zetta for something
steps.body: Describe a job in the chat. Zetta proposes the bots, and you approve them.

manual.summary: Prefer to do it by hand?
manual.body: These are the same steps the installer runs. The full list of settings is in apps/server/.env.schema.

items.a: A web app where bots work for you. You ask Zetta for a result, such as a daily briefing, a newsletter or a code review. Zetta sets up specialist bots, they do the work on your server, and you come back when there is a result or a decision for you.
Yes. Zetta is open source under the MIT license. You pay only for your own server and for the agents your bots use.
On your server, in a Postgres database that Zetta starts for you. Your chats, tasks and memory stay there.
Zetta has no AI model of its own and no bill for one. Each bot uses an agent installed on your server, such as Claude Code or Codex, and signs in the way that agent normally does.
Deleting files, administrator commands and sending email. Every change Zetta proposes is an Approve card too. Everything else runs on its own, and a blocked or uncertain result comes back to you.

items.q: Can I use it from my phone?
items.a: You can message your bots on Telegram, with your own bot token, or on WhatsApp, through your own WAHA server. Sending from WhatsApp is off until you turn it on.

items.q: Which systems does it run on?
items.a: The installer supports macOS, Linux and WSL, and needs Git, OpenSSL and a running Docker or Podman. On Windows, run it inside WSL.

cta.lead: One command on a server you control. Open source, MIT.

footer.tagline: Zetta: bots that do the work on your own server.
